doc.title: Joel Dorn interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2007

title: After Atlantic: Warner Brothers, the Midler fallout and Leon Redbone
summary: Dorn left Atlantic for Warner Brothers briefly. He was shaken by being thrown off the first Bette Midler album, then worked with Asleep at the Wheel, Don McLean and Leon Redbone.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans
story.community_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans

blocks.x: When you left Atlantic did you try to take any of those people with you?

Rahsaan and I went to Warner Brothers for a minute, Fathead was at Warner Brothers for a minute. But that was kind of it. I went off into another thing. I had had a really bad experience making that first Bette Midler record. They threw me off it and then the cuts that I made became the hits and then they wanted me to get back together and that really shattered me. ‘Cause with Nesuhi, he never changed what I did. But with Midler, Ahmet got involved and then all kinds of people that couldn’t find their way across the street with four compasses got involved. So I was embittered for a while and really thrown off. So I started making really — I mean I started working with Asleep at the Wheel, Don McLean, Lou Rawls, Steve Goodman, Peter Allen, and I made what I think are some very interesting, very good records. The biggest success I had was with a guy named Leon Redbone. And there’s another one nobody wanted. So it’s odd. Like I don’t really think about my career in terms of a career. When I do something like this, you know, where someone’s looking at me and asking me specific questions and I’m reminded of first of all what you think or what your view is of what I’ve done, and then I have my own view of it, which no one else in the universe could have, it’s odd at the end of it I have a body of work. By and large I’m pretty happy with it, you know it’s not all successful but nothing’s all successful. So like I think by and large I have a body of work you know.
You’ve done a lot of fantastic reissues. You must have a lot of patience. You don’t strike me as a real patient person but that’s my own observation.
